title: What I want, what I'm going to do
title_target: 뭐 하고 싶어요 — Mwo hago sipeoyo
goal: Talk about wishes and plans — the two things that free your conversation from what is happening right now and let it look ahead.
bekal: saying what you want with -고 싶어요
stating plans and guesses with -(으)ㄹ 거예요
telling the three apart and knowing when to use which
describing your weekend plans in a few sentences

dialogs.title: 대화 — Holiday plans
dialogs.intro: Minjun and Ani talk about an upcoming trip. Watch for the three future forms that appear here, and notice that none of them can replace the others.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Ani, what are you doing next week?
lines.literal: Ani — Ms., next — week-in — what — do-will — thing — is?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I'm going to Busan. I want to see the sea.
lines.literal: Busan-to — go-will — thing — is. sea — object — see — want.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: That sounds great! Are you going alone?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.literal: no, Suji — Ms. — with — together — go-will — thing — is.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: What do you want to do in Busan?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I want to go to Haeundae. And I want to eat raw fish.
lines.literal: Haeundae-to — go — want. and — raw-fish — object — eat — want.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Busan raw fish is really good. How many days will you stay?
lines.literal: Busan — raw-fish — as-for — really — tasty. how-many-days — stay-will — thing — is?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Three days. What about you, Minjun?
lines.literal: three — day — stay-will — thing — is. Minjun — Mr. — as-for — what — do-will — thing — is?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: I'll just be at home. I have a lot of work.
lines.literal: I — as-for — home-at — stay-will — thing — is. work — subject — much.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh, really? Then I'll bring you back a souvenir.
lines.literal: ah, so — is? then, gift — buy — will-come.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Really? Thank you! Have a safe trip.

notes: **-고 싶어요 is only for yourself.** It expresses the **speaker's** wish and can't be used for a third person's wish. "He wants to go" is not 그 사람은 가고 싶어요 but 그 사람은 가고 싶어**해요** — a different form. In questions, -고 싶어요? is used as is.

**-(으)ㄹ 거예요 covers two things at once: plans and guesses.** 갈 거예요 can mean "I'm going to go" (a plan) or "he'll probably go" (a guess about someone else). Context tells them apart, and in practice it almost never confuses anyone.

**-(으)ㄹ게요 is different from -(으)ㄹ 거예요, and the difference matters.** 갈게요 is **a promise or a decision just made in response to the other person**; 갈 거예요 is a plan that already existed. When Ani says 선물 사 올게요, she decides on the spot, in response. If she said 선물 사 올 거예요, it would sound like a long-standing plan with nothing to do with Minjun — much like English "I'll get you something" versus "I'm going to buy souvenirs."
**⚠️ -(으)ㄹ게요 is first person only, and statements only.** There is no 갈게요? as a question, and no 그 사람이 갈게요. When in doubt, -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is always safe.
**좋겠어요 means "that must be nice" or "lucky you".** It's the guessing form of 좋다, used to share in someone else's good news. It comes up constantly in conversation and has no one-word equivalent.

**다녀오세요 is said to someone who is leaving and expected back.** Literally "go and come back". It's said whenever someone leaves the house, goes to work or sets off on a trip. The person leaving answers 다녀오겠습니다.
**조심해서 means "carefully".** The -아서/어서 form here means "in the manner of", and it's covered fully in the last unit. For now, learn 조심해서 다녀오세요 whole, as a single goodbye.

**Counting days uses Sino-Korean numbers + 일.** 삼 일 = three days. ⚠️ Don't mix it up with 사흘 (the native Korean form, now less and less common) or with 삼 일 meaning "the third (of the month)". Context saves you, and even young Koreans often use the Sino-Korean form for both.

grammars.title: -고 싶어요 — saying what you want
body: Attach **-고 싶어요** straight to the verb stem. No choice of forms, no exceptions, whether the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant.
after: **The object can take 을/를 or 이/가.** 밥**을** 먹고 싶어요 and 밥**이** 먹고 싶어요 are both correct. 이/가 puts a little more weight on the thing itself and often sounds more natural with verbs of wanting.
**To negate, 안 also works:** 안 가고 싶어요. But -고 싶지 않아요 sounds a bit softer, and it's the one more often used to say no.

grammars.title: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 — plans and guesses
body: Attach **-ㄹ 거예요** if the stem ends in a vowel, **-을 거예요** if it ends in a consonant. Note that ㄹ is written into the last syllable block.
after: **거 is a shortened 것 ("thing")**, so 갈 거예요 is literally "it is a thing that will go". Knowing this makes the form much easier to remember than learning it as a blind ending.
**It's pronounced *gal kkeoyeyo*, not *gal geoyeyo*** — tensing after ㄹ. This is one of the forms beginners mispronounce most often.

grammars.title: Three futures, one table
body: The difference isn't time but **where the decision comes from**.

head: Form
Example
When to use
Who
rows: an existing plan, or a guess
a decision just made, a promise

after: Compare three answers to the same question, 내일 올 거예요?: **오고 싶어요** = I want to come (but may not be able to). **올 거예요** = I'm planning to come. **올게요** = OK, I'll come (a promise, decided right now).
All three are correct and all three are different. If you want to promise someone something, **-(으)ㄹ게요** is the right one — and it sounds much warmer than the other two.

blocks.text: What you have now is enough to talk about the future, just as unit 7 trained you to talk about the past. The example below uses all three forms in turn.
이번 주말에 부산에 갈 거예요. 수지 씨하고 같이 갈 거예요. 해운대에 가고 싶어요. 바다를 보고 싶어요. 그리고 회를 먹고 싶어요. 삼 일 있을 거예요. 민준 씨한테 선물을 사 올게요.

blocks.title: Three questions that open long conversations
items: **주말에 뭐 할 거예요?** — What are you doing this weekend? The Friday-afternoon question everyone in Korea asks.
**뭐 하고 싶어요?** — What do you want to do? More open, good for deciding together.
**한국에서 뭐 하고 싶어요?** — What do you want to do in Korea? A question you're almost certain to be asked as a foreigner. Have three answers ready before anyone asks.
